## Temperance

> *Temperance interprets the data generating mechanism and then uses it to
> answer, with the help of graphics, the question(s) with which we began.
> Humility reminds us that this answer is always false.*

Every example chapter carries two questions on the same outcome and the
same covariates — a primary framing and its paired opposite. So there are
**two videos here, not one**. The first shows the DGM producing an
*outcome*; the second shows it producing a *causal effect*. Watching them
back to back is the point: the machinery is identical, and only the column
being filled changes.

### The primary (predictive) question

Courage left us with a fitted data generating mechanism:

$$\text{Net Worth}_i = 0.50 + 0.50 \cdot \text{Years in Office}_i + \epsilon_i
\qquad \epsilon_i \sim \text{Normal}(0, 3)$$

That formula is not yet an answer. It is a *machine for producing* answers,
and the difference matters more than any single number it emits. Before we
read anything off it, watch it run.

The video below has narration, so turn your sound on. **Watch the error
column.** The formula is identical in every row — same intercept, same
slope. The error is redrawn each time, and that redraw is the entire reason
the last act produces a spread rather than a single number.

```{=html}
<video controls preload="metadata" playsinline width="100%">
  <source src="preceptor_to_graph_easy.mp4" type="video/mp4">
  Your browser cannot play this video.
  <a href="preceptor_to_graph_easy.mp4">Download it instead.</a>
</video>
```

The table and the graph in that video are the same object at two moments.
Elizabeth Warren's row never stopped being one row of the Preceptor Table;
we simply ran it 220 times and drew the results. The spread is what the
model actually claims about her — not the 12.50 that the formula returns
when you ignore $\epsilon$, and not any other single number.

This is why the Preceptor Table stays faintly visible under the finished
histogram rather than fading out. The graph did not replace the table. It
is what the table becomes when you run it enough times.

### The paired (causal) question

The paired question asks what *another term in office* does to a senator's
net worth. Same outcome, same covariate, same fitted machinery — but now
the Preceptor Table needs two outcome columns instead of one, because each
senator has a net worth if re-elected *and* a net worth if they retire.

$$Y_i(1) = 0.50 + 0.50 \cdot \text{Years}_i + 3.0 + \epsilon_i
\qquad Y_i(0) = 0.50 + 0.50 \cdot \text{Years}_i + \epsilon_i'$$

The two errors are *independent draws*, not the same number reused, so
each senator's individual causal effect $Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$ varies rather
than being a fixed 3.0. That choice is what gives the last act something
to show; see the note in the build script's config block.

**Watch the greyed-out column.** In every row one of the two potential
outcomes is dimmed and italic. That is the branch the senator did not
live, and no amount of data collection will ever fill it in — the
fundamental problem of causal inference, sitting in a table cell. The
quantity that flies down to the graph this time is the *difference*
between the two columns, not either column on its own.

```{=html}
<video controls preload="metadata" playsinline width="100%">
  <source src="preceptor_to_effect_easy.mp4" type="video/mp4">
  Your browser cannot play this video.
  <a href="preceptor_to_effect_easy.mp4">Download it instead.</a>
</video>
```

Two things in that last act are worth pausing on. First, the effect has a
*spread*, exactly as the outcome did — the causal effect is not a single
number any more than the prediction was. Second, **the spread crosses
zero**, which is why the dashed reference line is there. The model does not
claim that another term always makes a senator richer; it claims a
distribution of effects whose centre happens to be positive.

That second point is the one students miss when a causal estimate is
reported as a lone coefficient. The video makes it unavoidable.

### Reading the answer

With that in hand, the Quantity of Interest is a summary of the
distribution the video just built, not a summary of the formula:

```r
# The QoI comes off the predictive distribution, not off the coefficients.
# In the real chapter this is where marginaleffects does the work.
```

## Reference: rules for the embed

Commentary, not chapter prose. Do not copy this section into a chapter.

**Use a ```` ```{=html} ```` code block, not a `::: {=html}` div.** Pandoc's
raw-attribute syntax applies to fenced *code blocks*; there is no such thing
as a raw fenced *div*. The div form fails quietly and badly: Quarto emits a
literal `<div class="{=html}">` wrapper, drops the closing fence into the
page as visible `:::` text, and terminates the raw HTML at the first bare
text line, so a `</video>` can go missing. Everything still "renders", which
is why this is easy to ship broken. The code-block form passes the block
through verbatim, bare text lines included.

`![](video.mp4)` does not work at all. The raw block is the only form, and
it works unchanged inside a learnr tutorial too — which is the point, since
the same video ships in both artifacts.

`controls` is required. Nobody can replay the error-draw beat without a
scrub bar, and that beat is the one carrying the argument.

**No `loop` and no `muted`.** Both were correct when this animation was
silent and are wrong now. `muted` starts the voiceover switched off, which
is the whole feature disabled by default; `loop` restarts a 95-second
narrated explanation on top of itself the moment it ends.

Hard-tier chapters (13–16) swap in the shorter cuts
(`preceptor_to_graph_hard.mp4`, `preceptor_to_effect_hard.mp4`), which
assume the reader has already met the mechanism and are reinforcing
aggregation rather than teaching the arithmetic. Only the filename changes.

Both framings come out of one build script at four renders — predictive
and causal, each at two paces. Do not fork the script to add a framing;
see `animations.md`, section 3.
